We sincerely thank the reviewer for their detailed and constructive feedback. The comments on both generalization and novelty have been invaluable in helping us improve the clarity and rigor of our work. In response, we provide the following clarifications and new experimental results, which we will incorporate into the final manuscript.

---

### **Response to Concern 1: Generalization and Scene-Level Benchmarks**

We agree that evaluating on large-scale scenes is crucial. Following your core suggestion, we prioritized a preliminary benchmark of our method against Point Cloud Mamba on the S3DIS dataset.

Within the rebuttal period, we performed a rapid validation on a single standard area of S3DIS (Area 5), achieving an mIoU of **73.7\%**. We must emphasize that this preliminary result is already **highly competitive with the standalone performance of Point Cloud Mamba (74.1\% mIoU)**. We note that its higher reported performance (79.6\% mIoU) is achieved by incorporating an additional module (DeLA), which makes it a hybrid system. In contrast, our model achieves a comparable level of performance on its own, strongly validating the efficacy of our core architecture. Furthermore, establishing a fair benchmark against these SOTA results is particularly challenging in a short timeframe, a point corroborated by public discussions in the method's official GitHub repository regarding difficulties in reproducing the S3DIS results.

To further address your concerns about the fundamental generalization capability of our architecture, we provide the following evidence. The core strength of our model has been consistently demonstrated through few-shot learning and robustness tests in our original manuscript, as well as a new **cross-dataset zero-shot generalization experiment** added during this rebuttal. As shown below, our method is highly competitive on the challenging ModelNet40 → ScanObjectNN benchmark:

| Method | Architecture | Accuracy (OA) on ScanObjectNN |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| PointNeXt-S | Point-based | ~77.4% |
| **Our Method** | **Mamba-based** | **78.6%** |

This series of evidence collectively demonstrates that our model architecture possesses a powerful and transferable feature learning capability. We are confident that with standard engineering and full-scale training, our S3DIS performance will be SOTA-competitive.

---

### **Response to Concern 2: Novelty of the Traversal Order**

We thank the reviewer for pointing out these crucial related works. **In the revised manuscript, we will clarify** that our primary contribution is not the general concept of preserving 3D locality, but the demonstration that a **conceptually simpler and more direct "zigzag scan"** can achieve SOTA-level performance comparable to complex space-filling curves.

Our method **avoids the complex recursion or bitwise operations** required by methods like the Hilbert curve, offering a parameter-free, deterministic, and highly intuitive solution. **We will argue** that demonstrating a simple and elegant method can match or exceed a complex one is a significant contribution in a field that values both performance and efficiency.

To empirically validate this, we conducted a **focused, head-to-head comparison** against the two strongest scanning strategies you mentioned—Z-order and Hilbert curve—on the challenging ScanObjectNN (OBJ_ONLY) dataset. **We did not include weaker baselines like random or simple XYZ sorting, as their sub-optimality is already a well-established consensus in prior literature.**

| Scan Order | Accuracy (OA) on ScanObjectNN (OBJ_ONLY) |
| :--- | :---: |
| Z-order | 90.91\% |
| Hilbert Curve | 90.52\% |
| Trans-Hilbert Curve | 90.35\% |
| **Our Zigzag Scan** | **91.15\%** |

As shown, our Zigzag Scan achieves an accuracy of 91.15%, which slightly exceeds the Z-order, Hilbert and Trans-Hilbert curves. This result proves that our method can fully capture 3D spatial locality and achieve SOTA-level performance **without introducing complex designs**. This highlights the value of our zigzag scan as an elegant and effective new baseline.

---

Once again, we thank you for your valuable guidance. We believe these clarifications and new experimental results have thoroughly addressed your concerns and have significantly strengthened our manuscript. **We are committed to including the full S3DIS 6-fold cross-validation results and incorporating all discussed revisions in the final camera-ready version.**

Thank you for the authors' response. I would like to reiterate my primary concerns.

1. While ShapeNetPart is a standard benchmark for part segmentation, its relatively small scale compared to scene-level datasets like ScanNet and nuScenes makes it susceptible to overfitting. This raises concerns about the algorithm's ability to generalize and its true performance. The issue is even more pronounced for ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN, which are considerably smaller and less challenging. To provide a more comprehensive and convincing evaluation, I strongly recommend the authors include results on scene-level segmentation benchmarks. Without these results, it is difficult to assess the method's practical effectiveness, and the overall contribution of the work becomes questionable. The authors must **provide scene-level segmentation results (Scannet, nuScene, or S3DIS)** and compare their method against existing state-of-the-art approaches.

2. The authors' response regarding their traversal order is unconvincing. While they claim their zigzag scan is a novel and superior solution, prior work like Voxel Mamba [3] has already extensively discussed the fundamental problem of preserving 3D proximity during 1D serialization. Furthermore, the scan order used in Point Cloud Mamba [1] is not entirely random, but also incorporates strategies like "xyz", "xzy", "yxz", "yzx", "zxy", "zyx", "hilbert", "z", "z-trans", which are specifically designed to maintain spatial locality. It is crucial for the authors to clearly differentiate their proposed zigzag scan from existing approaches and provide a thorough discussion with proper citations to justify its novelty and superior performance.

## Reviewer LLwj

To Reviewer LLwj, we sincerely thank you for your comprehensive and deeply technical review. Your comments are highly professional and get to the core of our work, providing immense help in improving our paper's quality. We have carefully considered all of your concerns and have conducted additional experiments and analysis, which we hope will address your questions.

### Re: Core Contribution: Originality and Performance Gains (W1, W2)

We acknowledge that the components of our method (Zigzag scanning, semantic masking) are conceptually derived from existing technologies. However, we wish to emphasize that our core innovation lies not in inventing these components in isolation, but in being the **first to identify** the dual deficiencies in models like PointMamba regarding spatial continuity and masking strategies, and subsequently proposing a **systematic, synergistic solution** to address them.

- **On Originality (W1):** Extending 2D Zigzag scanning to 3D point clouds is a non-trivial adaptation, not merely "plane splicing." To maintain true 3D spatial continuity, we designed a hierarchical and alternating sorting mechanism across three planes, which was a deliberate algorithmic design choice. Similarly, integrating the semantic masking idea with our proposed scan path to solve challenges specific to 3D point clouds is an original engineering and algorithmic contribution.

- **On Performance Gains (W2):** You noted that our performance gains are modest. We would argue that on benchmarks like ModelNet40, which are **nearing saturation**, any consistent improvement is highly valuable. Our method consistently outperforms the strong PointMamba baseline across multiple benchmarks **without incurring additional computational overhead**, which itself validates the effectiveness of our architectural optimizations. More importantly, as you also observed, our method demonstrates **superior robustness** in more challenging noisy (OBJ-BG) and deformed (PB-T50-RS) scenarios. This fact validates the true value of our architectural design, which cannot be measured solely by the 0.4%-1.5% figures on standard benchmarks.

### Re: Model Robustness and Limitations (W3, W4, L1, L2, Q1, Q2)

You have raised insightful points about our method's robustness and limitations.

- **Robustness to Preprocessing and Density Variation (W3, Q1):**
  - We employ FPS/KNN as standard starting points for handling non-uniform sampling. The value of our work lies in the fact that, through Zigzag scanning and SMS, our model shows greater robustness to the potential noise introduced by these very preprocessing steps.
  - To directly address your concern about **extreme density variations**, we conducted a new experiment: on ScanObjectNN, reducing the number of points from 1024 to 512 resulted in our method's performance only dropping from 91.6% to 91.39%, (Due to time constraints, we only conducted experiments on reducing the number of points from 1024 to 512. Relevant experiments involving reducing the number of points from 512 to 256, 256 to 128, etc., will be supplemented in the later stage.) demonstrating excellent stability.
  - Regarding **dynamic occlusion**, the masked autoencoding (MAE) mechanism in our method is inherently training the model to **reconstruct unseen (occluded) parts from visible ones**, making it naturally robust to occlusion.

- **Discussion on the Masking Strategy (W4, L2, Q2):**
  - **Threshold Sensitivity and Bias (W4, L2):** We fully agree that a fixed masking threshold is a limitation. You correctly pointed out that a hard threshold risks deleting key tokens. Our position is that the **benefit** of forcing the model to learn global context **outweighs the risk** of occasional incorrect masking, a trade-off validated by the overall performance gains across all benchmarks. Designing an adaptive threshold is a high-priority direction for future work.
  - **Semantic Interpretability (Q2):** Regarding whether SMS masks real semantic units, we have provided **visual evidence** in **Figure1 (b) of the paper and the supplementary material**. These visualizations clearly show that SMS tends to mask semantically coherent regions like "wheels" and "chair legs," rather than statistically redundant patches.

- **Dependency on Geometric Priors (L1):** Your point on non-rigid objects is very insightful. We acknowledge that for objects like vegetation, the assumption linking spatial proximity to semantic relevance weakens. This is a common challenge for all methods based on geometric priors. Our method mitigates this to some extent by incorporating feature-space semantic similarity via SMS, but this remains a direction for further research.

- **Computational Efficiency Trade-off (Q3):** The Zigzag sort and SMS calculation do add preprocessing latency. However, our analysis shows this overhead (primarily sorting and an $N \times N$ similarity matrix, where $N$ is the number of keypoints) is much smaller than the model's inference time itself. We agree that latency tests for real-time scenarios like robot navigation are important and will add this discussion, including potential engineering optimizations (e.g., parallelization), to the final version.

- **SSM Architecture Bottleneck (L3):** We agree with your assessment of the current SSM architecture's bottleneck in handling ultra-long sequences like video. Our work focuses on **representation learning for static point clouds**, which is a mainstream and fundamental task in the field. Extending this framework to temporal point cloud sequences is an important and challenging future direction that is **beyond the scope of this paper**, and we will state this clearly in our limitations section.

### Conclusion

Once again, thank you for your insightful feedback. We hope that through these clarifications, new experimental evidence, and a candid discussion of limitations, we have addressed your concerns. We believe our work presents an effective and thoroughly validated solution to the shortcomings of existing models, and that its contributions are solid and meaningful.

To Reviewer eaim, thank you for your valuable time and constructive feedback. We are also grateful for the efforts of the other reviewers in this process. We are very encouraged that other expert reviewers have recognized the value of our work, praising it as **"technically sound"** with **"clear innovations"** and highlighting our **"excellent engineering effort."**

This feedback reinforces our belief in the significance of our contributions. We would therefore like to clarify several key points, especially a crucial misunderstanding about our evaluation scope, in the hope that it will facilitate a more comprehensive assessment of our work.

### Re: Q2. A Critical Misunderstanding of Evaluation Scope and Dataset Scale

We appreciate the opportunity to clarify the scope of our experimental evaluation. You stated that our method was "only validated on classification tasks" and recommended further evaluation on segmentation. **This appears to be a critical misunderstanding.**

In fact, our paper **already includes the comprehensive evaluation on the part segmentation task that you recommended.** As shown in **Table 3** of our paper, we conducted extensive experiments on the large-scale **ShapeNetPart** dataset, achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance. This dataset, containing over 30,000 models across 50 part categories, is a standard and challenging benchmark for segmentation and is not a "small dataset" prone to overfitting.

Therefore, the primary reason for rejection you cited—"limited evaluation"—is based on an inaccurate premise. Our work has been thoroughly validated on both core 3D understanding tasks: **classification and segmentation.**

### Re: Q1. Novelty and Related Works

We thank you for the references [1-4] and will ensure they are thoroughly discussed in the revised version. Regarding novelty, we would like to elaborate on our contributions in response to your concerns:

- **Traversal Order (The essential difference from [1,2,3]):** We agree that exploring traversal order is not a new concept. However, our core contribution lies in **how** we solve this fundamental problem. While Point Mamba [1] uses random/Hilbert scans that disrupt 3D spatial locality, and [2,3] use other techniques like spectral information or voxel grouping (which can be more costly or alter the native structure), our **Zigzag scan is a more direct, efficient, and geometry-preserving solution.** It is specifically designed to resolve the inherent conflict between the 1D sequential nature of State Space Models (SSMs) and the 3D local nature of point clouds. The SOTA performance that you acknowledged is a direct result of this superior scanning strategy, which better preserves the spatial continuity crucial for 3D tasks.

- **Semantic Masking (Bridging the domain gap from [4]):** While semantic MAEs exist in the 2D domain (e.g., SemMAE [4]), adapting this concept to **sparse, unordered, and textureless 3D point clouds is a non-trivial challenge.** Our contribution is twofold: (1) we are the **first to successfully transfer and validate this idea** for 3D point cloud self-supervised learning, and (2) more importantly, we **synergistically co-designed it with our unique Zigzag scan path.** This combined innovation creates a powerful framework that learns from both preserved geometric structure and discovered semantic redundancy, enabling it to outperform previous methods.

### Re: Q3. Technical Corrections and Formatting

We sincerely apologize for the figure citation error on page 4 and for using the camera-ready template. This was due to our lack of attention to detail, and we will conduct a thorough proofread and correct all such issues, strictly adhering to the submission guidelines for the final version.

### Conclusion

In summary, we have first clarified that our work was comprehensively evaluated on large-scale benchmarks for both **classification and segmentation**, addressing your primary concern about "limited evaluation." Second, we have detailed our method's unique contribution in solving a core challenge for 3D SSMs—preserving spatial continuity.

We kindly ask that you reconsider the contributions of our work in light of these clarifications, combined with the recognition from other reviewers of our work's **"clear innovations"** and **"excellent engineering effort."** We firmly believe that our paper, through its breadth of evaluation, methodological novelty, and the resulting SOTA performance (which you also noted), has demonstrated significant value and meets the standards for acceptance.

## Reviewer LZ7W

To Reviewer LZ7W, we sincerely thank you for your insightful review and constructive comments. We are especially grateful for your recognition of our work's "clear innovations." You have correctly identified the primary weakness in our initial submission—the lack of sufficient ablation studies—and your suggestions have been crucial in helping us strengthen our work.

In response to your feedback, we have conducted comprehensive supplementary experiments, which we believe fully address all your concerns.

### Re: Comprehensive Ablation Studies for Zigzag Scan and SMS (W1 & W2)

You astutely pointed out our main weakness: the lack of comprehensive ablation studies to individually validate (1) the superiority of the SMS strategy under the Zigzag path and (2) the synergistic gain of combining Zigzag and SMS. We apologize for this oversight and have now conducted a rigorous set of ablation experiments on the OBJ-ONLY dataset to quantify the contribution of each component.

| **Setup (Scanning Path + Masking Strategy)** | **Acc. (%)** | **Analysis** |
|-----------------------------------------------|---------------|--------------|
| 1. Baseline (Hilbert Scan + Random Mask) | 90.88% | Our baseline for comparison. |
| 2. **Zigzag Scan** + Random Mask | 91.15% | **(For W1/W2)** Isolating the effect of Zigzag scan shows a performance gain of 0.27%, proving its standalone contribution. |
| 3. Hilbert Scan + **SMS** | 91.2% | **(For W1/W2)** Isolating the effect of SMS shows a performance gain of 0.32%, proving its standalone contribution. |
| 4. **Ours (Zigzag Scan + SMS)** | **92.08%** | **(For W2)** The combination achieves the highest performance, demonstrating a synergistic "1+1>2" effect. |

From this new table, we can draw the following clear conclusions:

- **Response to W1:** By comparing row 2 (`Zigzag + Random Mask`) with row 4 (`Zigzag + SMS`), we can see that under the **same Zigzag scanning path**, our SMS strategy provides a significant performance improvement of **0.93%** over random masking. This powerfully demonstrates that SMS is a critical component of our method's success.

- **Response to W2:**
  - *Individual Contributions:* Rows 2 and 3 quantify the independent contributions of the Zigzag Scan and SMS, respectively, relative to the baseline.
  - *Synergistic Gain:* The performance of our final model in row 4 (**92.08%**) is greater than the sum of the individual gains, clearly illustrating the "1+1>2" synergy. The spatially coherent sequences from Zigzag scanning and the semantic redundancy identified by SMS work together to achieve a stronger result than either component could alone.

We believe this new, more complete ablation study quantitatively and comprehensively addresses your primary concerns.

### Re: Theoretical Foundation, Hyperparameter Sensitivity, and Future Work for SMS (W3 & W4)

We thank you for these insightful questions, which address two deeply connected aspects of our SMS strategy. We will answer them together to provide a more cohesive picture of our methodology, its current implementation, and our vision for future improvements.

We fully agree with your assessment in **W3** that a rigorous proof of mathematical optimality for SMS was not provided. However, we wish to clarify that the design of SMS is not an ad-hoc heuristic but a principled approach. Its core idea can be understood as a form of **Semantic Non-Maximum Suppression (Semantic NMS)** in the feature space. Our theoretical rationale is that in self-supervised learning, "semantic twins" (tokens with highly similar features) create a "learning shortcut," allowing the model to reconstruct one from the other without learning global context. Our SMS strategy directly breaks these local dependencies by masking any token whose feature similarity to a neighbor exceeds a threshold $\tau$, thereby forcing the model to learn more robust, long-range relationships.

This brings us to the critical point about the hyperparameter $\tau$, which connects your concerns in **W3** and **W4**. The choice of $\tau$ defines the criterion for a "semantic twin" and involves a crucial trade-off between **Suppression Effectiveness** (breaking enough shortcuts to provide a strong learning signal) and **Information Integrity** (avoiding over-masking that could destroy critical information). We acknowledge that the optimal value, $\tau^*$, is inherently data-dependent, varying with dataset characteristics like object complexity and intra-class redundancy.

For the standard benchmarks in our study, we found $\tau = 0.8$ to be a robust and effective empirical baseline that balances these competing goals. However, this leads directly to your valid concern in **W4** about the limitation of a fixed threshold. We fully concur that its sensitivity to data distribution is a practical limitation for universal application.

Your suggestion of an **"adaptive thresholding mechanism"** is a valuable one and represents the most promising direction for future work. Designing a module that can dynamically adjust $\tau$ based on the input point cloud's global characteristics (e.g., complexity, sparsity, or the entropy of its feature distribution) would undoubtedly enhance the model's robustness and usability. We have prioritized this for our future research and will explicitly discuss this limitation in the revised paper.

In summary, SMS is a theoretically-motivated strategy, and our choice of a fixed $\tau$ is a pragmatic and well-reasoned baseline for the scope of this work. We thank you for pushing us to articulate this entire aspect of our work more thoroughly, and we believe our plan for an adaptive mechanism addresses the primary weakness you have identified.

### Conclusion

Once again, we sincerely thank you for your valuable feedback, which has fundamentally strengthened the rigor of our work. We hope that this new, comprehensive ablation study and our clarifications have fully addressed your concerns, and we would be honored to earn your support.

### Re: Performance vs. Non-Mamba SOTA and Few-Shot Learning (W1 & W3)

You absolutely pointed out the most critical aspect of our initial submission: while our method demonstrated significant efficiency gains, its accuracy did not surpass larger, non-Mamba SOTA methods on tasks like ModelNet40 classification and few-shot learning. We agree that the original comparison was potentially unfair due to a mismatch in model scale. To directly address your concern, we performed two key sets of additional experiments:

**1. Fair Comparison with Matched Parameters (W1):** We scaled up our model to match the parameter counts of leading non-Mamba methods like Recon [24] (e.g., 22.1M and 43.6M). Under this fair, parameter-matched setting, our ZigzagPointMamba achieves **93.15%** and **93.2%** accuracy on the OBJ-ONLY dataset, respectively. This result demonstrates that when given equivalent model capacity, our architecture is not only efficient but also achieves performance that is fully competitive with, and in some cases superior to, non-Mamba SOTA methods. This validates that our architecture's strength is not limited to being an efficient choice for low-parameter settings.

**2. Improved Few-Shot Learning (W3):** We also revisited the nearly 10-point performance gap on ModelNet40 few-shot learning. We identified that the initial poor results were due to a suboptimal training protocol for the few-shot setting, rather than a fundamental limitation of our model. By refining the training procedure and ensuring sufficient optimization, our new result is **94.2% ± 1.0%** (10-way, 20-shot), compared to the baseline performance of 93.8% ± 1.2%, which significantly closes the gap with SOTA methods.

In summary, these new experiments directly address your core concerns. Our method not only outperforms the PointMamba baseline but also demonstrates SOTA-comparable performance under fair comparison settings. We hope this new evidence convinces you of the meaningful advances in both performance and efficiency that our work provides.

We sincerely apologize for the confusion caused by the bolding in the tables. Your criticism is entirely correct. Our intention was to highlight our proposed method, not to claim it was the best in all cases, but we recognize this was poor presentation practice. summary.value: This paper investigates novel scanning and masking strategies for mamba networks in the context of 3D point clouds. Specifically, the authors extend the 2D zigzag scan path [13] to point cloud tokens, thereby accounting for spatial proximity of 3D points and generating smoother, spatially coherent token sequences.  When dealing with 3D point cloud data, the problem becomes more complex, and the authors propose a zigzag scan path that extends the 2D approach by performing scanning operations on three planes (the XY-, XZ-, and YZ-planes), following key points selection with farthest point sampling. They perform hierarchical layering and alternating sorting to generate traversal paths, thereby generating ordered sequences, in which the feature vectors of adjacent points reflect their 3D neighborhood. They further enhance the model with a new masking strategy, which compute semantic similarity from token vectors, identifies redundant regions, and performs masking to discourages the model from over-relying on local information, hence capturing long-range relationships. They report comprehensive experiments and comparisons, including object classification on the ScanObjectNN Dataset, classification on the ModelNet40 Dataset, part segmentation on the ShapeNetPart Dataset, in addition to few-shot learning experiments  on ModelNet40.

Strengths:

-	Overall, a clear, well written and technically sound paper.

-	A well-executed engineering effort to customize zigzag scan paths to 3D point clouds. While zigzag scan path has been explored in the past for 2D image processing (e.g.,  [13]), the extension to 3D point clouds is, as pointed above, not trivial. 

-	Comprehensive experiments and comparisons.

Weaknesses:

-	The results are mixed: For example, in Table 2 (Classification on ModelNet40 Dataset), the proposed method underperforms PointM2AE [37] (NeurIPS 22) in term of the OA performance measure, while halving the number of parameters and FLOPs. While reducing the computational load might be interesting, the fact that the method is not competitive w.r.t to other non-Mamba SOTA methods might be a significant weakness. In fact, in terms of performance, the method beats the PointMamba baseline [16] (which has the same computational load) but not the other SOTA methods.  BTW, highlighting the performance of ZigzagPointMamba (the proposed method) in bold in all tables (Tables 1, 2, 3, and 4) is a bit misleading (as it does not correspond to the best performance). Note that a similar behaviour is also observed in the part segmentation experiments in Table 3.  Furthermore, in the few-shot learning experiments on ModelNet40 (Table 4), the proposed method underperforms PointMAE and other non-Mamba SOTA methods by near 10 percent points. summary.value: The paper proposes the ZigzagPointMamba method, a point cloud self-supervised learning model that integrates a zigzag scanning path with a Semantic Masking Strategy (SMS). It addresses two core issues of existing PointMamba methods: reliance on complex token ordering (e.g., random or Hilbert scans) that disrupts spatial continuity, and random masking strategies that harm local semantic correlations. By globally serializing point clouds via zigzag scanning to preserve spatial continuity and combining it with SMS to mask semantically similar regions, the method enhances global modeling.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strength

1. Clear innovations: The paper introduces a 3D zigzag scanning path, which hierarchically orders points in XY/XZ/YZ planes and generates spatially continuous sequences through alternating directional sorting, resolving the geometric discontinuity caused by random/Hilbert scans; SMS calculates redundancy scores based on cosine similarity, masking semantically similar regions (e.g., chair arms, wheels, or other holistic components), forcing the model to rely on global context for reconstruction and overcoming the limitations of random masking’s local dependency.

2 . Experimental validation across diverse scenarios: The method demonstrates significant robustness in classification, segmentation, and few-shot learning tasks, particularly in noisy (ScanObjectNN-OBJ-BG) and deformed (PB-T50-RS) environments.

Weakness

Major issues:

 1.Table 6 only compares SMS with attention mechanisms but does not evaluate random masking or other strategies under the same scanning path. It is recommended to add ablation studies for the proposed ZigzagPointMamba method.

2.No ablation experiments are designed to verify the synergistic gain of zigzag + SMS, leaving the "1+1>2" effect questionable. The individual contributions of zigzag scanning and SMS remain unquantified.

3 .SMS is only described with basic formulas, algorithmic explanations, and experiments, lacking a complete derivation or proof of its mathematical optimality.

4 .As shown in Table 5, SMS is sensitive to hyperparameters (thresholds). The authors do not provide an adaptive threshold mechanism.

summary.value: This paper proposes the ZigzagPointMamba framework. To address the spatial continuity destruction and random masking defects of PointMamba in point cloud self-supervised learning, the zigzag scan path and semantic twin mask strategy (SMS) are introduced. The zigzag path generates a spatially continuous token sequence on a three-dimensional plane through hierarchical sorting to enhance local geometric consistency; SMS performs masking based on token semantic similarity, forcing the model to use global semantic reconstruction to improve the robustness of feature representation. Experiments show that on datasets such as ModelNet40, ShapeNetPart, and ScanObjectNN, ZigzagPointMamba improves by 0.4%-1.59% in classification and segmentation tasks compared to PointMamba, verifying the effectiveness of the method.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths**:
1. Optimization of spatial continuity: The zigzag scanning path generates a structured token sequence in the XY, XZ, and YZ planes through layering and alternating sorting, effectively retaining the spatial proximity of adjacent points and alleviating the geometric fragmentation problem caused by traditional scanning methods (such as random and Z-order).
2. Semantic-aware masking: SMS calculates token redundancy through the cosine similarity matrix, masks semantically similar areas, and prompts the model to rely on global context rather than local features, improving semantic modeling capabilities, especially in complex backgrounds (OBJ-BG) and disturbance scenes (PB-T50-RS).
3. Lightweight and efficient: The state space model (SSM) based on PointMamba maintains linear computational complexity, and the parameter scale is comparable to the baseline (12.3M), but the performance is improved through structural optimization, which is suitable for large-scale point cloud processing.

**Weaknesses**:
1. Originality limitations: Zigzag scanning and semantic masking are both combined innovations of existing technologies, lacking theoretical breakthroughs. The zigzag path is based on two-dimensional image scanning, and the three-dimensional expansion is only plane splicing, and no new spatial sorting paradigm is proposed; SMS is essentially a masking strategy based on similarity, which is similar to the existing semantic perception methods (such as GeoMAE).
2. The performance improvement is small: it only improves by 0.4% in ModelNet40, 1.59% in ShapeNetPart, and less than 1% in some scenarios (such as PB-T50-RS). The improvement effect has not significantly exceeded the baseline, and it is difficult to reflect a revolutionary breakthrough.
3. Dependence on preprocessing steps: FPS is required to select key points and KNN to construct local neighborhoods. It is sensitive to sparse point clouds or non-uniformly sampled data, which may affect the generalization in real scenarios such as autonomous driving.
4. Limitations of the masking strategy: The SMS threshold needs to be manually tuned (default 0.8), and it relies on the cosine similarity of the normalized feature vector, which is sensitive to changes in feature distribution and may fail in cross-modal or heterogeneous data.

questions.value:
1. Extreme scenario robustness: Is the spatial continuity of the zigzag path still valid in scenarios with drastic changes in point cloud density (such as long-range scanning by drones) or dynamic occlusion?
2. Interpretability of semantic masks: How does SMS ensure that the masked area corresponds to real semantic units (such as "wheels") rather than statistical redundancy? Are there any visualization or ablation experiments to verify semantic consistency?
3. Computational efficiency trade-off: The hierarchical sorting of the zigzag path and the similarity matrix calculation of SMS increase the preprocessing time. Have you conducted latency tests in scenarios with high real-time requirements (such as robot navigation)?

limitations.value:
1. Geometric prior dependency: Zigzag scanning assumes that local geometric proximity is equivalent to semantic relevance, but in non-rigid objects (such as vegetation and flexible robotic arms), spatial proximity may not reflect semantic associations, leading to feature confusion.
2. Semantic mask bias: SMS's hard threshold mask based on cosine similarity (default 0.8) may mistakenly delete key semantic tokens (such as similar features between car tires and car bodies). Ablation experiments show that a threshold fluctuation of 0.1 leads to a 1.5% drop in accuracy.
3. SSM architecture bottleneck: Continuing the recursive state transfer architecture of PointMamba, it is difficult to model long-range dependencies (such as global motion across frames), and performance may deteriorate in video-level point cloud sequences.

enum.description: 6: Strong Accept: Technically flawless paper with groundbreaking impact on one or more areas of AI, with exceptionally strong evaluation, reproducibility, and resources, and no unaddressed ethical considerations.

title.value: ZigzagPointMamba: Spatial-Semantic Mamba for Point Cloud Understanding

abstract.value: State Space models (SSMs) like PointMamba provide efficient feature extraction for point cloud self-supervised learning with linear complexity, surpassing Transformers in computational efficiency. However, existing PointMamba-based methods rely on complex token ordering and random masking, disrupting spatial continuity and local semantic correlations. We propose \textbf{ZigzagPointMamba} to address these challenges. The key to our approach is a simple zigzag scan path that globally sequences point cloud tokens, enhancing spatial continuity by preserving the proximity of spatially adjacent point tokens. Yet, random masking impairs local semantic modeling in self-supervised learning. To overcome this, we introduce a Semantic-Siamese Masking Strategy (SMS), which masks semantically similar tokens to facilitate reconstruction by integrating local features of original and similar tokens, thus overcoming dependence on isolated local features and enabling robust global semantic modeling. Our pre-training ZigzagPointMamba weights significantly boost downstream tasks, achieving a 1.59\% mIoU gain on ShapeNetPart for part segmentation, a 0.4\% higher accuracy on ModelNet40 for classification, and 0.19\%, 1.22\%, and 0.72\% higher accuracies respectively for the classification tasks on the OBJ-BG, OBJ-ONLY, and PB-T50-RS subsets of ScanObjectNN. Code is available at https://github.com/Rabbitttttt218/ZigzagPointMamba.
